config.title: N-Queens

intro.title: N-Queens
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a program that solves the N-Queens lesson, which involves placing N chess queens on an N×N chessboard so that no two queens threaten each other. You will learn to implement a backtracking algorithm, a core programming concept that explores possible solutions step-by-step and undoes choices when they lead to a dead end. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays for representing the board and recursion for exploring placements. By the end, you'll understand how to systematically solve constraint-based lessons using this fundamental algorithmic approach.
intro.usecase: The N-Queens backtracking algorithm pattern appears in real-world scheduling and resource allocation systems, such as conference room booking interfaces where multiple meetings must be placed without time conflicts. Product managers use similar constraint-solving logic in dashboard filters that prevent overlapping date ranges or mutually exclusive options. This pattern also powers interactive seating chart tools for events, ensuring guests are placed according to social distancing or grouping rules without violating proximity constraints.

objectives: Construct a function to validate queen placements on a chessboard.
Implement a recursive backtracking algorithm to explore board configurations.
Apply the algorithm to solve the N-Queens lesson for a given board size.
Initialize and manipulate a 2D array to represent the chessboard state.
Render a visual representation of a valid N-Queens solution.
Integrate validation checks within the backtracking process to prune invalid placements.
Configure the solution to return all distinct board configurations for N.

content.body: Imagine placing queens on a chessboard so none can attack each other. This classic puzzle teaches a powerful lesson-solving technique. Today you'll learn how to systematically explore possibilities and backtrack when needed.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain when and why backtracking is needed
• Implement the try → explore → undo pattern
• Solve the N-Queens lesson using backtracking
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a 4×4 board. Try placing queens one row at a time. Place your first queen in row 0, column 0. Where can you safely place the next queen in row 1?
content.title: Try placing queens
content.visualMetaphor: Explore a path; if it dead-ends, go back and try another branch.

content.body: Great! You placed a queen safely in row 1. Now try row 2. Can you find a safe spot? If not, what should you do?
content.title: Continue exploring

content.body: You've reached a point where no safe spot exists in the current row. This is a dead end. What's your next move?
content.title: Hit a dead end

content.body: You tried placing queens systematically, but when you hit a dead end, you naturally wanted to go back and try different placements. That's the essence of backtracking!
content.title: What you experienced

content.body: For a 4×4 board, you can mentally track placements. But for 8×8 or larger boards, we need an algorithmic approach. We need to systematically try options and know when to backtrack.
content.title: Why we need a system

content.body: Backtracking follows a simple pattern: try a choice, explore deeper with recursion, then undo if it doesn't lead to a solution. We explore all options by undoing failed attempts and trying different branches.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Like exploring a maze: go down one path; if it's a dead end, go back to the last junction and try another path.

content.body: We'll place queens row by row. For each row, we try every column. If a placement is safe, we place the queen and recurse to the next row. If we reach the end, we found a solution. If we hit a dead end, we backtrack by removing the last queen and trying the next column.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start from the first row
2. For each column in the current row:
   • Check if placing a queen here is safe
   • If safe: place queen, move to next row
   • If reaches last row: record solution
   • If unsafe or dead end: backtrack (remove queen)
3. Continue until all possibilities explored

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the N-Queens solution using backtracking. Remember: backtracking is try → explore → undo. When you hit a dead end, undo the last choice and try another path. This pattern works for many constraint satisfaction lessons like Sudoku, maze solving, and permutation generation.
